title: a16z Frontier | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z renames its crypto fund 'a16z Frontier' and widens it to any long-horizon technology — AI-native products, autonomous machines, full-stack startups and machine-to-machine networks — arguing that blockchains are receding into infrastructure (stablecoin and programmable money rails) and that companies should be defined by what they do, not the tech they use.

themes.theme: Crypto fund becomes a Frontier fund

insights.claim: a16z is renaming its crypto fund 'a16z Frontier' and widening it to any startup building new technologies and creating markets that may take years to develop, while continuing to invest in crypto and advocate for sensible crypto regulation.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: A leading crypto VC franchise is diversifying its mandate; read it as a signal that crypto-only venture capital is no longer a distinct category.

insights.claim: Blockchain infrastructure has receded into the background as Wall Street and fintech firms launch blockchain-based products, so labeling companies by the technology they use matters less than what they do.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Crypto is being absorbed into mainstream financial infrastructure; the 'crypto company' label loses value as an investing screen.
insights.quote: It makes more sense to define companies by what they do rather than by the technologies they use.
insights.locator: When we started investing in crypto

insights.claim: The fund's leadership is Chris Dixon with Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz and GPs Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet, with operating teams supporting portfolio companies on regulatory, go-to-market, talent, marketing and technical R&D.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Names who is deploying the capital and with what support model.

insights.claim: Dixon's long-horizon investing has followed two themes since 2013: new computing devices enabled by cheaper smartphone-era cameras, sensors and chips (Oculus, Skydio, Zipline), and crypto as a new wave built on social media and open source (Coinbase, Solana, Uniswap).
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Shows a16z's repeatable playbook: back technologies that look futuristic well before they reach the mainstream.

insights.claim: Crypto networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum gained traction 'from the outside in' because social media let communities form without first needing mainstream acceptance, and open source supplied the model of software anyone can inspect, modify and build on, which blockchains extended to services and networks.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Explains the a16z origin thesis for crypto; useful for judging which new tech waves can bootstrap without institutional permission.
insights.locator: Social media allowed networks like Bitcoin and Ethereum

insights.claim: Early applications of a new technology tend to do old things better; AI so far has mostly made existing activities like coding and knowledge work faster, better and cheaper, but 'native' use cases — brand-new activities — will follow.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: The big AI value creation may sit in categories that do not yet exist, which are hard to size or screen for today.
insights.quote: Early applications of new technologies tend to focus on doing old things better.
insights.locator: Foremost is the emergence of native use cases

insights.claim: Native AI experiments will initially look strange and unserious, like toys and hobbies, and the way to tell which will become mainstream is to understand their potential rates of improvement — the factors that bend deceptively marginal growth into an exponential curve.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: A screening heuristic for early-stage AI bets: underwrite the improvement rate, not current seriousness.
insights.locator: At first, many of these experiments will look strange

insights.claim: a16z sees early signals of a post-AGI world in which software and increasingly hardware become easier to create, and expects a proliferation of new devices — autonomous machines that perceive, reason and act physically, biology- and medicine-linked devices, and hybrids — to underpin this cycle as smartphones did the last.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Points to robotics, physical AI and bio-hardware as the hardware leg of the AI cycle.
insights.locator: We're lucky enough to be living through one of the most consequential curves

insights.claim: AI and new capabilities will favor full-stack startups combining software with hardware and services, as founders seek new forms of defensibility, and increasingly autonomous AI agents may change what it means to be a founder and how industries are organized.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Expect defensibility to come from integrated stacks rather than pure software layers.
insights.locator: All these advances will present new ways of building companies

insights.claim: AI will enable new kinds of networks connecting people and intelligent agents that learn, coordinate, produce and transact; networks built for machines will look very different from today's human-built networks, often starting as single-player tools that evolve into multiplayer networks.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent networks are named as a major untapped category — a watch item for platform and protocol plays.
insights.locator: AI will also enable entirely new kinds of networks

insights.claim: Blockchains give the internet money rails that are fast, cheap, global and programmable; stablecoins are becoming a standard tool for fintechs and established institutions, and crypto can give new networks native economic capabilities and machine-to-machine transactions.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Stablecoin rails are positioned as the settlement layer for AI agents; connects crypto adoption to the AI buildout.
insights.locator: Blockchains will play a significant role in this transformation

insights.claim: The defining companies of past technology waves were rarely the ones anyone predicted, so a16z frames its examples as illustrations, not boundaries, and expects founders to create categories not yet imagined.
insights.speaker: Chris Dixon
insights.so_what: Argues against narrow thematic mandates; supports a wide-net early-stage approach.
